reason: The person needs the code on GitHub main as reviewable feature commits, and was repeatedly failed by lumped commits and uncommitted work. The agent must commit per feature, never mix tickets, and pull and push when asked.

A pull during this episode hit a CHANGELOG.md conflict with a concurrent upstream commit. The agent kept both entries, then re-verified the merged code before pushing; that sequence should be the stated procedure.

The person had to say "you are supposed to do that automatically" when finished tickets stayed uncommitted after the completion commit landed. The skill says completions commit but not what to do when they do not, so the agent reached for hand-committing.
After the person rejected a test run, the agent committed and pushed an unrequested change, suppressed the push's stderr, then reported "pushed" without checking the result.

An agent edited a finished ticket's prompt file after the completion, saw the skill say completions commit themselves, reverted its own edit, and routed the fix to the peer ticket editing the same file. That routing is the rule the skill does not yet state for a fix found after completion.
Ticket branches carry the shared checkout's uncommitted files via a snapshot commit; reviews fail on it. Rule for merging ticket branches.

The episode's push silently published 25 other commits along with its own two-file fix; the commit rules forbid pushing what the person did not ask for, but nothing tells the agent to look at what a plain push will carry.

A done ticket's fix was reported as shipped while its second commit was still only on the ticket branch; the skill says completion commits land themselves but not that they stay off main until merged.

Ticket #98's landing was blocked by untracked roundtable record copies in the main checkout; the diagnosis (git refuses to overwrite untracked files on merge) and the byte-compare check before moving them aside are durable landing knowledge absent from this skill.

An agent committed a landing change whose subject was a single ~400-character sentence, with the ticket numbers and rationale inline; a peer's note on the same day named oversized commit messages in merge.py as a live problem. The git-commits skill has no subject-length rule, so the next commit repeats it.
